summary.text: Chebyshev's inequality gives an upper bound on the probability that a random variable with finite variance strays far from its mean.
The chance of deviating from the mean by more than kσ is at most 1/k², where σ is the standard deviation.
It applies to any distribution whose mean and variance are defined, but it often gives a poor bound compared with what extra knowledge allows.

facts.label: Two deviations
facts.value: At least 75% of values lie within two standard deviations

facts.label: Three deviations
facts.value: At least 88.88% lie within three standard deviations

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: Pafnuty Chebyshev, though Bienaymé formulated it first

facts.label: Needs
facts.value: A distribution with a defined mean and variance

items.prompt: Journal articles in a collection average 1000 words, with a standard deviation of 200. Knowing nothing else about the shape, what can you say about articles between 600 and 1400 words?

options.label: At least three quarters of them fall in that range
Exactly half of them fall in that range
Fewer than a quarter fall in that range
Almost none fall outside that range

items.explain: That range is two standard deviations either side of the mean, so no more than 1/4 can lie outside it.

items.prompt: You know a data set's average and spread but have no idea what shape it has. Why use Chebyshev's inequality instead of the 68-95-99.7 rule?

options.label: It always gives a tighter answer than the rule
The rule only works for small samples
The rule applies only to normal distributions
It does not need the average or spread

items.explain: The 68-95-99.7 rule holds only for normal distributions, while Chebyshev's inequality works for a broad range of distributions.

items.prompt: Chebyshev's bound guarantees at least 75% within two deviations, yet in your data 95% lie there. Is that a contradiction?

options.label: Yes, since your data break the inequality
Yes, since the inequality demands exactly 75%
No, since it only needs to hold for the data
No, since it is a minimum that is often loose

items.explain: The inequality states a guaranteed minimum for broad families of distributions, and it often gives a poor bound compared to what more knowledge shows.

items.prompt: Someone applies the inequality with k equal to 1 and finds the chance of straying beyond one standard deviation is at most 1. Is that useful?

options.label: No, probabilities are always at most 1 anyway
Yes, it proves no value can stray that far
Yes, it shows everything stays within range
No, because k must be a whole number over 5

items.explain: When k is 1 or less, the bound is 1 or more, and since every probability is at most 1 the statement is trivial.

items.prompt: Could Chebyshev's inequality be used for a distribution whose variance is not finite?

options.label: Yes, since only the average is needed
No, it requires a finite variance
Yes, if k is chosen large enough
No, it works only on normal shapes

items.explain: The inequality is stated for a random variable with finite variance, so it cannot be used when the variance is undefined.

items.prompt: A student says the Chebyshev bound is always strictly bigger than the true probability. Is that right?

options.label: Yes, because it is only ever an overestimate
Yes, since equality would break the theorem
No, since the true probability is always larger
No, as some random variables make it exact

items.explain: The inequality is tight: for each chosen constant, there exists a random variable for which it is an equality.
